newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australian dlr puts budget behind it, pares losses.
newsitem.headline: Australian dlr puts budget behind it, pares losses.

text.p: The Australian dollar edged up from early lows at the midsession as the market resigned itself to being disappointed with the budget and attempted to shift back to fundamentals.

It was hampered somewhat, however, by government attempts to to portray the budget as a force for lower interest rates. This was not welcomed by dollar bulls who had thought the easing question had been buried by the Reserve Bank governor last week.
Indeed, many analysts felt the RBA would not have been impressed by the laxity in the budget and if anything it would have reinforced the bank's inclination to keep rates steady.

By 12.15 pm (0215 GMT) the local dollar had ventured to US$0.7775/80 after spending much of the morning pinned at US$0.7760 support, but was still well short of the US$0.7826/31 level enjoyed before the budget was released on Tuesday.

Chart watchers said the resilience of support would encourage die-hard bulls but the currency needed to clear US$0.7835 resistance if it was to avoid a further protracted period of aimless range trading.
The dollar also regained a little ground on the crosses as US$/yen made a choppy rally and rumours of trouble at a couple of trust banks raised concerns about Japan's financial system.
Some of the worries surrounded Sumitomo Trust Bank which was suspended on the Tokyo stock exchange this morning as talk circulated it was planning to issue 100 billion yen of shares.
These occasional signs of underlying weakness in the banking system tend to aid both dollars as it strongly suggests the Bank of Japan will not hike rates and thus risk bank failures.
The yen wavered for a moment and the dollar crept up to
92.45/55 yen from an early 91.74 low, but again was still short of Tuesday's late 93.20/30.
In trade weighted terms the currency was down at 59.5 from a previous 59.9 finish.
Dealers said part of the market's adverse reaction to the budget was on the assumption it was not tight enough to win a credit upgrade for Australia this year.
That fear was confirmed this morning with both Moody's and S&P saying the budget was not enough to trigger an upgrade.
Longer term, analysts were somewhat mollified that the budget was projected to reach an underlying surplus in 1998/99 and beyond, a performance unmatched by most OECD countries.
The Westpac consumer sentiment index for May at 2.30 pm will provide a distraction and provide an up-to-the-minute reading of the consumer sector. -- Wayne Cole 61-2 9373 1800
